questions.title: Normal RBC count, adult males
questions.question: The normal RBC count for adult males is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 6-8.5 million/mm3 is well above the normal adult range and would suggest polycythaemia, not a normal count.
explanations.B: Correct. The normal RBC count for adult males is 5-5.5 million/mm3. This is higher than the female range because androgens stimulate erythropoiesis and males lack the cyclical menstrual blood loss that lowers the female range. A count outside this range, in the absence of any other explanation, is what first raises suspicion of anaemia or polycythaemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 4.5-5 million/mm3 is the normal range for adult females, not males.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 4-4.5 million/mm3 is below even the normal female range and would suggest a mild anaemia in an adult male.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 3.5-4 million/mm3 is clearly in the anaemic range for an adult male.

questions.learning_objective: State the normal adult male RBC count reference range.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.118 (Physio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q29); corroborates author1's erythrocyte-physbank.json phys-9 hold from HIS 1-MCQ-scan.pdf p.3

questions.title: Normal RBC count, adult females
questions.question: The normal RBC count for adult females is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 6-8.5 million/mm3 is well above the normal range for either sex and would suggest polycythaemia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 5-5.5 million/mm3 is the normal range for adult males, not females.
explanations.C: Correct. The normal RBC count for adult females is 4.5-5 million/mm3. This is lower than the male range because females lack the androgen-driven erythropoietic stimulus and lose blood cyclically with menstruation. Pregnancy lowers the count further still, through plasma-volume expansion diluting the same red cell mass.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 4-4.5 million/mm3 is below the normal female range and would suggest a mild anaemia.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 3.5-4 million/mm3 is clearly in the anaemic range for an adult female.

questions.learning_objective: State the normal adult female RBC count reference range.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.118 (Physio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q30); corroborates author1's erythrocyte-physbank.json phys-10 hold from HIS 1-MCQ-scan.pdf p.3

questions.title: Normal haemoglobin content, adult males
questions.question: The normal haemoglobin content for adult males is:

explanations.A: Correct. The normal haemoglobin content for adult males is about 15-16 gm/dL, of which about 96-98% is HbA. This is higher than the female range for the same androgen-driven erythropoietic reason behind the RBC count difference between the sexes. Values below this range, in an otherwise well male, prompt a work-up for anaemia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 17 gm/dL is above the normal adult male range and would suggest polycythaemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 19 gm/dL is the level normal newborn infants reach because of relative intrauterine hypoxia, not the normal adult male range.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 10 gm/dL is well below the normal adult male range and would represent anaemia.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 12 gm/dL is also below the normal adult male range and would represent anaemia.

questions.learning_objective: State the normal adult male haemoglobin content reference range.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.119 (Physio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q31); corroborates author1's erythrocyte-physbank.json phys-14 hold from HIS 1-MCQ-scan.pdf p.4

questions.title: Normal haemoglobin content, adult females
questions.question: The normal haemoglobin content for adult females is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 17 gm/dL is well above the normal adult female range and would suggest polycythaemia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 19 gm/dL is the level normal newborn infants reach, not the normal adult female range.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 10 gm/dL is below the normal adult female range and would represent anaemia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 12 gm/dL is also below the normal adult female range and would represent a mild anaemia.
explanations.E: Correct. The normal haemoglobin content for adult females is about 13-14 gm/dL. This is lower than the male range for the same androgen/menstrual-loss reasons behind the RBC count difference between the sexes. Newborn infants, by contrast, reach up to 19 gm/dL because of relative intrauterine oxygen deficiency, a level neither adult sex normally reaches.

questions.learning_objective: State the normal adult female haemoglobin content reference range.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.119 (Physio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q32); corroborates author1's erythrocyte-physbank.json phys-15 hold from HIS 1-MCQ-scan.pdf p.4

questions.title: Chain composition of adult haemoglobin (HbA)
questions.question: Which of the following haemoglobin types contains 2 alpha and 2 beta chains?

explanations.A: Correct. Adult haemoglobin, HbA, is a tetramer of 2 alpha and 2 beta globin chains and makes up about 96-98% of total adult haemoglobin. This 2-alpha/2-beta pairing is what a question means whenever it names "normal adult haemoglobin" without further qualification.
explanations.B: Incorrect. HbA2 pairs 2 alpha chains with 2 delta chains, not 2 beta chains, and makes up only about 2-4% of adult haemoglobin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. HbF (fetal haemoglobin) pairs 2 alpha chains with 2 gamma chains, giving it a higher oxygen affinity than adult HbA — a different pairing from the one this question asks for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Immunoglobulin is an antibody protein with no haem group and no globin-chain structure at all; it is unrelated to hemoglobin's chain composition.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Myoglobin is a single-chain, single-haem protein found in muscle, not a tetramer, and so cannot be described by a "2 and 2" chain pairing.

questions.learning_objective: Identify HbA as the 2-alpha/2-beta haemoglobin tetramer that makes up most adult haemoglobin.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.114 (Physio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q10); same fact repeated identically at p.117 Q23

questions.title: Chain composition of fetal haemoglobin (HbF)
questions.question: The structure of fetal haemoglobin (Hb F) consists of 4 polypeptide chains:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 2 alpha and 2 beta chains describe HbA, the adult form, not HbF.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 2 alpha and 2 delta chains describe HbA2, a minor adult haemoglobin (about 2-4%), not HbF.
explanations.C: Correct. Fetal haemoglobin, HbF, is a tetramer of 2 alpha and 2 gamma globin chains. Its gamma chain binds 2,3-BPG less tightly than the adult beta chain does, giving HbF a higher oxygen affinity than HbA — the mechanism that lets the fetus pull oxygen across the placenta from the mother's own, lower-affinity, adult haemoglobin. HbF predominates before birth and is largely replaced by HbA by about four months of age.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Theta" is not a globin chain used in any normal human haemoglobin type.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Kappa" is an immunoglobulin light-chain type, not a haemoglobin globin chain.

questions.learning_objective: Identify HbF as the 2-alpha/2-gamma haemoglobin tetramer, and explain why its chain composition gives it a higher oxygen affinity than adult HbA.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.116 (Physio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q18); corroborates author1's erythrocyte-physbank.json phys-16 hold from HIS 1-MCQ-scan.pdf p.4

questions.title: Average diameter of an RBC
questions.question: Which is the average diameter of an RBC?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 40 micrometres is roughly the size of a large cell such as a megakaryocyte, far larger than a red blood cell.
explanations.B: Correct. The mature erythrocyte's average diameter is about 7.5 micrometres, corresponding to a mean corpuscular volume of about 87-95 cubic micrometres. This small size, together with the cell's biconcave, deformable shape, is what lets it squeeze through capillaries narrower than its own resting diameter without rupturing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 20 micrometres is closer to the size of a monocyte, the largest normal cell in a peripheral blood smear, not an RBC.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 3 micrometres is closer to a platelet's size (2-4 micrometres), not an RBC's.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 10 micrometres is closer to the size of a neutrophil or lymphocyte, not an RBC.

questions.learning_objective: State the average diameter of a mature erythrocyte.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.104 (Physio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q1); resolves author1's erythrocyte-physbank.json phys-2 hold (RBC diameter/MCV, no matching concept found in that pass)

questions.title: Major function of RBCs
questions.question: The major function of RBCs is:

options.A: Carriage of oxygen from the lungs to the tissues
options.C: Haemoglobin as an excellent acid-base buffer
options.D: Increasing blood viscosity and peripheral resistance

explanations.A: Correct. The major function of the erythrocyte is carriage of oxygen from the lungs to the tissues, bound to haemoglobin. Every other function on this list is real but secondary — none of them is what the red cell mass exists primarily to do.
explanations.B: Incorrect. RBCs do carry some CO2 (partly as carbamino-haemoglobin), but most CO2 transport is as plasma bicarbonate; this is a secondary contribution, not the major function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Haemoglobin's acid-base buffering is real but secondary to its oxygen-carrying role, which is why it is not the answer described as the "major function."
explanations.D: Incorrect. RBCs do contribute to blood viscosity, but this is an incidental physical consequence of the red cell mass, not a function the erythrocyte exists to perform.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Iron storage is the role of ferritin and haemosiderin, mainly in the liver, spleen and bone marrow, not a function of the circulating erythrocyte.

questions.learning_objective: Identify oxygen carriage as the major function of the erythrocyte, as distinct from its secondary contributions to CO2 transport, buffering and viscosity.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.118 (Physio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q28); resolves author1's erythrocyte-physbank.json phys-7 hold

questions.title: RBC morphology in iron deficiency anaemia
questions.question: The red cells in iron deficiency anaemia are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Macrocytic (large) red cells with normal haemoglobin content describe megaloblastic anaemia (folate or B12 deficiency), not iron deficiency.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Normocytic normochromic red cells describe anaemias of marrow depression or acute blood loss, where cell size and haemoglobin content per cell are unchanged, not iron deficiency.
explanations.C: Correct. Iron deficiency anaemia produces microcytic (small, MCV under 80 cubic micrometres) hypochromic (pale, low Hb content per cell, MCH under 25 pg) red cells. Insufficient iron limits haemoglobin synthesis during erythropoiesis, leaving each new cell both smaller and paler than normal. This is the pattern that distinguishes iron deficiency from the normocytic and macrocytic anaemias caused by other mechanisms.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Normocytic hypochromic is not the classic iron-deficiency pattern; iron deficiency's defining feature is a reduced cell size (microcytic) together with reduced haemoglobin content (hypochromic).
explanations.E: Incorrect. Spherocytic red cells describe hereditary spherocytosis, a membrane defect causing haemolysis, not the cell shape produced by iron deficiency.

questions.learning_objective: Identify iron deficiency anaemia's red cells as microcytic and hypochromic, and distinguish this from the megaloblastic and normocytic patterns.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.116 (Physio HIS 1 past-exam block, Q16)
